name: WKKC 89.3 FM
description: WKKC 89.3 FM is the noncommercial educational radio station of Kennedy-King College, owned by the City Colleges of Chicago and broadcasting from the college's Englewood campus at 6301 S. Halsted Street. On air since 1975 — its construction permit issued August 5, 1975, after an objection from Northwestern University's WNUR forced a resubmission, and its power raised from 10 to 250 watts in 1985 — the station trains Black broadcasting students while serving Chicago's South Side. Its Friday Night Audio mix show became one of the city's longest-running: a college-radio home for house music after WBMX's Hot Mix 5 era faded and life-changing airtime for local hip-hop artists, hosted in its defining years by PinkHouse. Block Club Chicago's 2026 history calls WKKC a Black radio powerhouse that brought house music to the masses. Today the station broadcasts an urban format in HD Radio — urban adult contemporary on HD1, classic hip hop on HD2 — and counts footwork pioneer DJ Rashad among the artists who worked its boards.

name: Walter Payton
description: Walter Payton (July 25, 1954, Columbia, Mississippi – November 1, 1999) — 'Sweetness' — was the Chicago Bears running back whose thirteen seasons set the endurance and production standard for his position. At Jackson State University, a historically Black university, he rushed for more than 3,500 yards and broke the NCAA scoring record with 65 rushing touchdowns. Drafted fourth overall by Chicago in 1975, he played his entire career with the Bears, missing only one game, and retired as the NFL's all-time leading rusher with 16,726 yards, 110 rushing touchdowns, and 21,803 all-purpose yards. On November 20, 1977, he ran for a then-record 275 yards in a single game against Minnesota. In the 1985 season he helped lead the Bears to their fifteen-win campaign and a 46–10 victory over New England in Super Bowl XX. He entered the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1993; the league's Man of the Year award now bears his name.

name: What's Going On
description: What's Going On is Marvin Gaye's eleventh studio album, released on May 21, 1971, by Tamla, the Motown Records subsidiary label. Recorded in Detroit and California studios in 1970–71, it was Gaye's first album to credit him as producer and the first to credit Motown's in-house session band, the Funk Brothers. It is a concept album and song cycle whose songs mostly segue into one another, narrated from the viewpoint of a Vietnam veteran returning home to hatred, suffering, and injustice; its lyrics take up drug abuse, poverty, the war, and, in 'Mercy Mercy Me,' ecological harm. The album held No. 1 on Billboard's Soul LPs chart for nine weeks, and its title track, 'Mercy Mercy Me (The Ecology),' and 'Inner City Blues (Make Me Wanna Holler)' all reached the Hot 100 top ten. It entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1998 and topped Rolling Stone's revised 2020 list of the 500 greatest albums.

description: Wizkid, born Ayodeji Ibrahim Balogun on 16 July 1990 in the Ojuelegba area of Surulere, Lagos, Nigeria, is a Nigerian singer and songwriter who became a central voice of the Afrobeats generation. He began recording at age eleven with church friends in the group the Glorious Five and signed to Banky W's Empire Mates Entertainment in 2009. His debut album Superstar (2011) made him a national star, and Ayo (2014) carried "Ojuelegba," the record that carried his name abroad. His fourth album, Made in Lagos (2020), produced "Essence," featuring Tems, which became the first Nigerian song to reach the Top 10 of the Billboard Hot 100, peaking at No. 9. name: Warner Saunders
description: Warner Saunders (January 30, 1935 – October 9, 2018) was a Chicago television journalist whose four-decade career made him one of the defining anchors of Black Chicago broadcasting. A Chicago native, he held a bachelor's degree from Xavier University of Louisiana and a master's degree from Northeastern Illinois University, and he worked first as a public school teacher, youth worker, and Boys Club executive director before entering television. At WBBM-TV he served as director of community affairs and hosted the talk program Common Ground and the children's program known as The Good Gang Express. He then spent 29 years at NBC 5 (WMAQ-TV) as a sports and then news anchor, retiring in May 2009. His reporting included a 1990 series from South Africa on the release of Nelson Mandela, gathered into a documentary, and coverage spanning the aftermath of Martin Luther King Jr.'s assassination, Harold Washington's 1983 mayoral campaign, and the rise of Barack Obama. He was a past president of the Chicago chapter of the National Association of Black Journalists and a member of the Chicago Journalism Hall of Fame. He died in Chicago on October 9, 2018, at age 83.

name: Woodlawn
description: Woodlawn is an official Chicago community area on the South Side, east of Washington Park and south of Hyde Park. The 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in adjacent Jackson Park brought an estimated 20,000 new residents and a building boom of hotels, apartment buildings, and wood-frame houses stretching west from the lake along the 63rd Street tram lines. By the early 1950s Woodlawn's color line had broken under Black migration after World War II, and restrictive covenants had been struck down in the late 1940s. In 1963 The Woodlawn Organization, led by Rev. Arthur M. Brazier, defeated the University of Chicago's Woodlawn expansion plan — a documented civic victory in CTL's corridor brief. The neighborhood's transit history is contested ground: on September 27, 1997, the elevated structure east of Cottage Grove was demolished with less than 24 hours' public notice, over community objection led by Brazier. Woodlawn also holds the Washington Park National Bank Building at 6300 S. Cottage Grove, opened in 1924. Tier is R: the graph record's only source is a Wikipedia community-areas page.

name: WVON
aliases: WVON 1690; The Voice of the Negro
description: WVON — ‘The Voice of the Negro,’ later ‘The Voice of the Nation’ — is Chicago’s historic Black radio station, the canonical record of the WVON cluster (facets: CTL-E-1316, the listened-to institution; CTL-E-1377, the Midway Broadcasting business; CTL-E-0782, the aircheck archive). Leonard and Phil Chess bought WHFC-1450 and launched WVON on April 1, 1963; its ‘Good Guys’ DJs made it the civil-rights-era voice of Black Chicago, broadcasting through the unrest after Dr. King’s 1968 assassination. After Leonard Chess’s death the family sold the station to Globetrotter Communications (sale consummated 1970), which moved it to the 5,000-watt 1390 signal on February 5, 1975; Gannett followed in 1977. In 1979 Pervis Spann and Wesley South’s Midway Broadcasting bought the dormant 1450 license (launching as WXOL; the WVON calls returned March 28, 1984), converted the station to all-talk in 1986, and on September 18, 2006 moved WVON to 1690 AM, where it broadcasts today. The U.S. and Illinois Houses honored its 50th anniversary in 2013.

name: WJPC
description: WJPC was Johnson Publishing Company's Black-owned radio station on Chicago's 950 AM. Johnson Publishing bought the frequency's WGRT in May 1973 for $1.8 million, and the call letters became WJPC on November 1, 1973 — a change documented in a contemporary Jet item of November 15, 1973. CTL's Johnson Publishing dossier describes WJPC as the first Black-owned Chicago radio station, and its president and general manager Marv Dyson — per his HistoryMakers oral-history finding aid — discovered Tom Joyner in Montgomery, Alabama, and brought him into Chicago radio. The station began nighttime operation in 1980, flipped to an all-rap format on July 15, 1992, and was sold by Johnson Publishing in December 1994, ending the Black-owned era on 950 AM that CTL's radio brief traces from WGRT's 1967 soul format through WJPC's two decades. The call letters are the owner's initials' company made audible: WJPC was Johnson Publishing Company, broadcasting.

The paper is female-owned; its publisher is Denise Rolark Barnes, the founder's daughter, who took over the family business. Its stated mission is to 'educate, inspire and inform — and to publish positive news about African Americans.' It began as part of the Fund for Black Journalism, founded by the Local Media Association and the ten papers, with seed backing that included a Walton Family Foundation grant and a $300,000 Google News Initiative Innovation Challenge grant. Incubated inside the Local Media Foundation, it converted on January 1, 2024, when its assets were sold to a newly formed public benefit corporation — the first national Black news collaboration to adopt that structure.

name: WPP
description: WPP is a London-based global advertising holding company. In CultureTechLens research, its significance for Black media history is its June 2000 strategic alliance with UniWorld Group, the New York multicultural advertising agency founded in 1969 by Byron Lewis and one of the oldest African American-owned agencies in the United States. WPP acquired a 49% interest in UniWorld, which continued to operate as a separate, autonomous business. UniWorld — rebranded UWG in 2014 — remains minority-owned and woman-led, headed by CEO Monique L. Nelson, with WPP still holding its 49% as strategic partner. The MEDIA-001 research uses the deal to illustrate how legacy Black agencies survived by partnering with, and partially ceding ownership to, mainstream conglomerates.

Lomax Jr. bought the 900 AM station; the purchase year is disputed in CultureTechLens's sources, given as 2001 in the station's own OnWURD podcast account and as 2003 in Wikipedia's account of his daughter, Sara Lomax-Reese, who became the station's president and CEO, expanded it to 96.1 FM in 2017, and co-founded URL Media. description: The White City Ballroom was the ballroom of the White City Amusement Park at 63rd Street and South Park Avenue (now Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Drive), on the Woodlawn / Greater Grand Crossing edge of the South Side. The park opened on May 26, 1905 (one Illinois history source gives May 27 — a minor contradiction the corpus notes), spread over fourteen acres, and rivaled Coney Island; its ballroom was built for 1,000 dancers, alongside the College Inn restaurant seating 2,500. The graph record describes it as a big-band ballroom within White City, and the University of Chicago's jazz guide — the record's source — documents the ballroom in Chicago Defender citations, including a Wolfscale's Band appearance on June 22, 1918 and a White City advertisement on July 2, 1921, with the room operating into the 1920s–1940s. The park fell into financial distress and bankruptcy in 1933–34 and most of it closed in 1934; its roller rink survived, renamed Park City Roller Rink, until 1958, and the site was later occupied by Parkway Gardens. description: The African-American women mathematicians who worked as human 'computers' at the NACA Langley Research Center's segregated West Area, 1943-1958, performing flight-test and aeronautical calculations by hand.

name: William Young
description: Inland Steel mill worker at Indiana Harbor who became a Steel Workers Organizing Committee leader — elected vice-president of the merged Lodge 1010 in 1938 and the first Black chair of a steel union local grievance committee.

name: World News Service
description: Chicago-based Black wire service founded by Hiram E. Jackson circa 1960–1961. News releases survive for 1961–1963 in the Claude A. Barnett Papers, filed alongside Associated Negro Press releases (1928–1964). A thinly documented service operating in the ANP's final years.

name: William C. Linton
description: Founder, editor, and publisher of The Chicago Whip (1919-1922); his paper's 'Don't Spend Money Where You Can't Work' campaign won jobs for over 15,000 Black Chicagoans. Atlanta-born son of AME minister Rev. T. J. Linton; came to Chicago in 1917.

name: Woodlawn Property Owners Association
description: Group of white South Side businessmen that organized a racially restrictive covenant for the South Park subdivision in 1928.

description: Long-running Black-format station (1955- ) on Chicago's airwaves: R&B as WBEE, jazz from 1968, gospel as WBGX since 2003; brokers time to Black churches. Ownership/control is disputed.

name: West Side Organization
description: Bottom-up economic organizing of unemployed people, tenants, and welfare recipients on Chicago's West Side in the 1960s. Directed by Chester Robinson, the WSO collaborated in the Chicago Freedom Movement, backed the 1966 Cicero march over SCLC objections, and allied with Operation Breadbasket, the Contract Buyers League, and street organizations in a grassroots mobilization network.

name: WVON radio as a listened-to Black Chicago institution
description: WVON-AM (‘Voice of the Negro,’ later ‘Voice of the Nation’) as Black Chicago listened to it, 1963–1979 — the reception facet of the WVON cluster (canonical station record CTL-E-0179; business facet CTL-E-1377; archive CTL-E-0782). The station launched April 1, 1963 (founding owned by CTL-E-0179; ownership chronology settled in conflict CTL-CFL-000123); its ‘Good Guys’ DJs quickly made it a civil-rights-era voice of Black Chicago. This record’s subject is the listening itself: how a Black-oriented station functioned as a daily institution in its audience’s life during the Chess and Globetrotter years.

name: Watching Soul Train (the Chicago years)
description: Saturday viewing of the Black dance/music show born in Chicago — appointment television for Black youth. Soul Train premiered locally on WCIU-TV in 1970, entered national syndication from Los Angeles in 1971, and ran 35 seasons to 2006. Era corrected from 1970–1975: production left Chicago in 1971 (see conflict CTL-CFL-001854).

name: WVON 1450 AM / Midway Broadcasting Corporation
description: The business facet of WVON: Midway Broadcasting Corporation, formed in 1979 by former WVON DJs Pervis Spann and Wesley South, which purchased the dormant 1450 AM license that year (the station’s 1963 founding is owned by the canonical record, CTL-E-0179). Broadcasting first as WXOL, it recovered the WVON call letters in 1984, adopted an all-talk Black format in 1986, and in 1999 passed to the controlling interest of Melody Spann-Cooper, Midway’s chair and CEO. In 2006 Midway moved the station’s programming to 1690 AM under a lease-management agreement, where it operates today.

In 1966 it welcomed the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. and SCLC, becoming headquarters of the Chicago Freedom Movement's West Side campaign against slum housing.

name: Wayne Shorter
description: Wayne Shorter received the NEA Jazz Masters Fellowship in 1998. In CultureTechLens's label research he appears in the documented catalog history of Vee-Jay Records, the pioneering Black-owned label: Vee-Jay's jazz line, run from 1958 under A&R man Sid McCoy, carried Lee Morgan, Wayne Shorter, Eddie Harris, Wynton Kelly, and Paul Chambers — the last through the Sutherland Lounge and Miles Davis connection. That catalog claim, graded Verified in the BMI-002 research package, is the one substantive corpus passage naming Shorter; he is otherwise present in CTL's record through the NEA roster and his cataloging as CTL-JAZZ-066 in the CTL-JAZZ-100 dataset of African American jazz artists (2026).

name: What Color Is Love
description: What Color Is Love is a studio album by Terry Callier, released in 1972 on Cadet Records, the Chess Records subsidiary. Produced by Charles Stepney, it is the centerpiece of Callier’s Cadet trilogy: music that moves between folk guitar, jazz harmony, and soul orchestration, carrying “Dancing Girl,” the title track, and “You Goin’ Miss Your Candyman.” The album sold little on release, and Callier’s Cadet years ended when Chess was sold; the records survived instead through British Northern soul and acid-jazz dancefloors, where “You Goin’ Miss Your Candyman” became a club staple and was later sampled by Urban Species. Some discographies date the album 1973; CTL follows the 1972 Cadet dating carried by Wikipedia’s discography and by CTL’s own album canon, and records the variance rather than hiding it. What Color Is Love is the fullest document of what the Chicago Songwriters Workshop generation could do when a major Black label gave a folk-soul writer an orchestra.

name: West Loop
description: The West Loop is the Near West Side industrial district west of Chicago's Loop where the Warehouse stood at 206 S. Jefferson Street. In the late 1970s it was a desolate former manufacturing area of loft and warehouse buildings, far from the established entertainment districts. That emptiness was functionally important to the club: the City of Chicago landmark report, drawing on Frankie Knuckles, notes the location suited a Black and gay clientele that was not welcome in the entertainment districts, and the district's sparse nighttime population made the club's very loud sound system survivable in a way a dense nightlife district would not have allowed.

name: William McBride
aliases: William Thacker McBride Jr.; William McBride Jr.
description: William Thacker McBride Jr. (September 27, 1912 – August 11, 2000) was a Chicago painter, designer, teacher, and collector — a mainstay of the South Side Community Art Center and of the Black Chicago art world that built it. Born in the Algiers neighborhood of New Orleans to vaudeville performers, he migrated with his family to Chicago's Bronzeville at about age ten, attended St. Elizabeth grammar school and Wendell Phillips High School, and took classes at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago in the early 1930s. He joined George Neal's Arts and Crafts Guild, worked for the Civilian Conservation Corps, and from 1935 found steady work with the WPA Federal Art Project's Illinois Art Project — designing posters, books, and costumes for the Federal Theatre Project. An early supporter of the South Side Community Art Center, his paintings appeared in its inaugural exhibition of December 15, 1940. He later worked for Goldblatt's department store, taught, agitated, and assembled one of the largest private collections of African and African American art of his generation. The Smithsonian's Archives of American Art recorded his oral history in 1988.

name: William C. Robinzine Sr.
aliases: Robie; William Robinzine; Bill Robinzine Sr.
description: William C. Robinzine Sr. (1932–2000), a guard known as “Robie,” was the first African American to play men's basketball at DePaul University. A Chicago South Sider who attended Wendell Phillips Academy High School, he began college at Xavier University in New Orleans, transferred home to DePaul, and sat out the 1953–54 season under NCAA transfer rules. As a junior in 1954–55 he averaged 15.0 points and 6.2 rebounds for a 16–6 Blue Demons team; as a senior he averaged 15.5 points for a 16–8 team that reached the NCAA Tournament and fell to Bill Russell's San Francisco. He played for Hall of Fame coach Ray Meyer, who told the Chicago Tribune in 2000 that Robinzine was “a very talented individual who played very well for us.” His son, Bill Robinzine, also played at DePaul (1972–75) and spent seven seasons in the NBA. Robinzine died on April 10, 2000, and was inducted into the DePaul Athletics Hall of Fame in 2001.

name: William Beavers
description: William M. Beavers (February 21, 1935 – October 26, 2024) was a Chicago Democratic politician who served 23 years as alderman of the 7th Ward and then as Cook County commissioner for the 4th District. Born in Chicago and raised in the Kenwood and Oakland neighborhoods, one of six children of a steel-mill worker, he attended Chicago public schools and Harold Washington College and served 21 years as a Chicago police officer before his election to the City Council in 1983. As alderman he chaired the Police and Fire Committee and later the Budget Committee, and he is credited in his family's account with creating judicial subcircuit districts that opened judgeships to Black lawyers on the South and West sides and in the southern suburbs. In 2006 he moved to the Cook County Board, where his daughter Darcel succeeded him in the 7th Ward. In March 2013 a federal jury convicted him of tax evasion; he was sentenced to six months in prison, and the Seventh Circuit upheld the conviction in June 2014. He died on October 26, 2024, at 89.

name: Way Up with Angela Yee
description: Way Up with Angela Yee is a nationally syndicated midday radio show hosted by Angela Yee, the Radio Hall of Fame personality who co-hosted The Breakfast Club from its December 2010 launch until her departure in 2022. Premiere Networks launched Way Up into national syndication on February 6, 2023; the four-hour show originates from iHeartMedia New York's Power 105.1 (WWPR-FM) and debuted on more than 30 iHeartMedia stations, a footprint later station pages put at more than 50. Built around music, celebrity interviews, and listener conversation, the show marked Yee's move from ensemble morning radio to a solo-branded program carrying her own name. CultureTechLens profiled the show in Short #83, published October 13, 2026; no entity record existed before this packet.

name: Wisdom Kaye
description: Wisdom Kaye (born Wisdom Uduebor, April 4, 2001, in Lagos, Nigeria) is a Nigerian-American model and fashion creator whom Vogue dubbed 'TikTok's best-dressed guy.' Raised in Houston, Texas, from age four, he enrolled at Texas State University to study electrical engineering before leaving to pursue fashion. He began posting editorial-style fashion videos to TikTok in January 2020; a viral Vogue Challenge run carried him to two million followers by July 2020. Scouted by IMG Models through social media, he made his runway debut at Balmain's Spring/Summer 2022 show and has since worked with Dior, Fendi, Ralph Lauren, Coach and Revlon. Teen Vogue named him to its 21 Under 21 list in 2021 and Forbes to its 30 Under 30 in Art & Style in 2023; he made his Met Gala debut in 2024, and in 2025 Forbes ranked him among its Top Creators and TIME placed him on its inaugural TIME100 Creators list. name: Will Bynum
description: Will Bynum, born William Bynum on January 4, 1983, in Chicago, Illinois, is an American former professional basketball player and coach. At Crane High School he was named Chicago Public Player of the Year in 2001. He played college basketball at Arizona (2001–03) and Georgia Tech (2003–05) before going undrafted in 2005. Bynum was the NBA D-League Rookie of the Year with Roanoke in 2006, played briefly for Golden State, and won an Israeli league championship and Finals MVP award with Maccabi Tel Aviv in 2007. His longest NBA tenure came with the Detroit Pistons from 2008 to 2014, followed by Guangdong in China, Washington in 2015, the Windy City Bulls in 2016–17, and a final stop in Turkey in 2018. He appeared in 360 NBA games, scoring 2,921 points, and in 2025 joined the Birmingham Squadron of the NBA G League as an assistant coach.

name: Wave Sports + Entertainment
description: Wave Sports + Entertainment is an American sports media company founded in 2017, headquartered in Santa Monica, California, that produces original sports programming for social, audio and video platforms. It began as WAVE.tv, a Los Angeles-based company built around short-form sports content for younger audiences, and raised 32 million dollars in a Series A round announced in 2020, led by CoVenture and GPS Partners. The company states that its programming serves more than 130 million followers globally. Its original series are led by athletes and media personalities and include 'New Heights with Jason and Travis Kelce,' '7PM in Brooklyn with Carmelo Anthony,' 'The Right Time with Bomani Jones' and 'Podcast P with Paul George.' Wave announced 'Podcast P' with NBA player Paul George in March 2023 as the newest addition to its portfolio; the weekly show, co-hosted by Jackie Long and Dallas Rutherford, is presented by Wave Sports + Entertainment. Through its Wave Media Agency division the company also works with leagues, teams and other sports properties on audience and revenue work across social platforms.

name: Wyclef Jean
aliases: Nelust Wyclef Jean; Wyclef; Toussaint St. Jean
description: Wyclef Jean, born Nelust Wyclef Jean on October 17, 1969, in Croix-des-Bouquets, Haiti, is a Haitian rapper, singer, songwriter and producer. He emigrated with his family at age nine to Brooklyn, New York, and settled in East Orange and Newark, New Jersey. He gained fame as a member of the Fugees, whose second album, The Score (1996), became one of the best-selling albums of all time, and launched a solo career with Wyclef Jean Presents The Carnival (1997), which carried the top-ten hit 'Gone Till November' and the Grammy-nominated 'Guantanamera.' His second album, The Ecleftic: 2 Sides II a Book (2000), included the hit '911' with Mary J. Blige, and he appeared on Shakira's 'Hips Don't Lie' (2006), a number-one single in eighteen countries. As a producer and writer he worked on Destiny's Child's 'No, No, No,' Whitney Houston's 'My Love Is Your Love' and Santana's 'Maria Maria.' His honors include three Grammy Awards, the BET Humanitarian Award and the NAACP Vanguard Award. Haiti appointed him Ambassador-at-Large in 2007; his 2010 candidacy for Haiti's presidency was ruled ineligible on residency grounds, and his Yéle Haiti charity later closed amid financial scrutiny.

name: Wallace Best
description: Wallace D. Best is an American historian of African American religion whose scholarship centers on Black Chicago. Princeton University's Department of Religion records that he joined the Princeton faculty in 2007, holds appointments in the Departments of Religion and African American Studies with a faculty affiliation in History, and serves as Director of the Program in Gender and Sexuality Studies; he holds the Hughes-Rogers Professorship of Religion and African American Studies. He earned his Ph.D. at Northwestern University. His first book, Passionately Human, No Less Divine: Religion and Culture in Black Chicago, 1915–1952, published by Princeton University Press, is described by the publisher as the first book-length analysis of the new religious practices and traditions in Chicago stimulated by the Great Migration, showing how Black southerners built a new sacred order that joined Southern folk religious sensibility to modern city life. Before Princeton, he taught at the University of Virginia from 2000 and joined Harvard Divinity School in 2004 as Assistant Professor of African American Religious Studies. His second book, Langston's Salvation: American Religion and the Bard of Harlem (New York University Press, 2017), won the American Academy of Religion's 2018 award in Textual Studies.

name: Wilt Chamberlain
aliases: Wilton Norman Chamberlain; Wilt the Stilt; The Big Dipper
description: Wilt Chamberlain, born Wilton Norman Chamberlain on 21 August 1936 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, was an American center whose records still define basketball's outer limits. A star at Philadelphia's Overbrook High School and at the University of Kansas, where he reached the 1957 NCAA final, he spent a season with the Harlem Globetrotters before joining the Philadelphia Warriors in 1959 and winning both Rookie of the Year and Most Valuable Player in his first season. On 2 March 1962 he scored 100 points in a single game, a record that still stands, and that season he averaged 50.4 points per game. He is the only player to average at least 30 points and 20 rebounds over an entire career, finishing with 31,419 points and an NBA-record 23,924 rebounds. Traded to the Philadelphia 76ers, he won his first championship in 1967, then moved to the Los Angeles Lakers in 1968, won a second title in 1972 and earned Finals MVP. A four-time league MVP and 13-time All-Star, he was enshrined in the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 1978. He died on 12 October 1999 in Los Angeles, California, at age 63.

Paul Vathis's 100-point dressing-room photograph (public domain) is documented as a verified alternative (§5); the Pennsylvania placard photograph depicts a roadside marker for the game, not the subject, and was rejected by name.

name: Warren Moon
description: Warren Moon (born November 18, 1956, Los Angeles) is the quarterback whose career exposed and then outlasted the NFL's refusal to draft Black quarterbacks. At the University of Washington he was named MVP of the 1978 Rose Bowl, yet no NFL team drafted him, so he began his professional career in Canada, leading the Edmonton Eskimos to five consecutive Grey Cup championships (1978–1982), a CFL record, and winning two Grey Cup MVP awards. He then played seventeen NFL seasons, principally for the Houston Oilers (1984–1993), with later stops in Minnesota, Seattle, and Kansas City before retiring in 2000. Moon was named to nine Pro Bowls, was the NFL's Offensive Player of the Year in 1990, and threw for 49,325 NFL passing yards. In 2006 he became the first Black quarterback, and the first undrafted quarterback, inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame; he remains the only player in both the Pro Football and Canadian Football Halls of Fame.

name: Willie Thrower
description: Willie Thrower (Willie Lee Thrower Sr., born March 22, 1930, New Kensington, Pennsylvania; died February 20, 2002) was the first Black quarterback to play in the modern National Football League. At Michigan State he was the first Black quarterback in the Big Ten and a member of the Spartans' 1952 national championship team. Signed by the Chicago Bears, Thrower made his NFL debut on October 18, 1953, against the San Francisco 49ers at Wrigley Field, relieving George Blanda and completing three of eight passes for 27 yards with one interception — the first appearance by a Black quarterback in the modern NFL, as the Bears' own history records it. The Bears released him after the 1953 season, and the league's color line at quarterback held for years more. Warren Moon thanked Thrower by name in his 2006 Pro Football Hall of Fame speech; a statue of Thrower was unveiled at his Valley High School in 2006.

name: Walter Mosley
description: Walter Mosley (born January 12, 1952, Los Angeles) is the novelist who brought the Black private-eye tradition into the literary mainstream with Ezekiel “Easy” Rawlins, the Watts factory worker turned reluctant detective. His debut, Devil in a Blue Dress (1990), set in 1948 Los Angeles, was named among the Mystery Writers of America's best hundred mystery novels and was filmed in 1995 with Denzel Washington as Rawlins. The Rawlins series has run for more than three decades alongside Mosley's Leonid McGill and Fearless Jones books, science fiction, plays, and essays. His publisher and the press describe him as the most important African American crime writer since Chester Himes, and he was a favorite author of President Bill Clinton. Mosley's work insists that the detective novel — America's most democratic form — belongs to Black Los Angeles as fully as to Chandler's.

name: Within Our Gates
description: Within Our Gates is a 1920 silent feature written, directed and produced by Oscar Micheaux, the earliest surviving feature by a Black director. Its story follows Sylvia Landry, a Black schoolteacher played by Evelyn Preer, who works to keep a Southern school for Black children open and travels north seeking funding, while flashbacks expose the racial violence of the Jim Crow South, including a lynching presented from a Black point of view. The Library of Congress National Film Registry essay describes the film as Micheaux's direct engagement with the most controversial aspects of American race, made in the shadow of The Birth of a Nation (1915). When Micheaux opened it in Chicago and Detroit in January 1920, authorities in several cities demanded cuts on the stated threat of unrest, and he could afford only four prints. Long considered lost, the film survives in a single print found in Spain under the title La Negra, with only four of its original intertitles remaining; the restored version carries reconstructed titles. The film was added to the National Film Registry in 1992.

name: Whoopi Goldberg
description: Whoopi Goldberg, born Caryn Elaine Johnson on November 13, 1955, in New York City, is a comedian, actor and producer whom Britannica describes as the first Black woman to achieve EGOT status — winning an Emmy, a Grammy, an Oscar and a Tony. She first came to national attention with a one-woman stage show of character monologues, brought to Broadway in 1984; a recording of that show won the Grammy Award for Best Comedy Album. Her film breakthrough came as Celie in The Color Purple (1985), which earned her a Golden Globe and an Academy Award nomination. She won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for Ghost (1990), becoming the second Black woman to win an acting Oscar, and headlined Sister Act (1992) and its sequel, at the time becoming the highest-paid actress in Hollywood. She completed the EGOT in 2002 with a Daytime Emmy and the Tony Award for producing Thoroughly Modern Millie. Since 2007 she has co-hosted and moderated the daytime talk show The View, and she has hosted the Academy Awards ceremony four times.

name: Wanda Sykes
description: Wanda Sykes (born Wanda Yvette Sykes, March 7, 1964, in Portsmouth, Virginia) is a stand-up comedian, actor and writer. Raised in Maryland, she graduated from Hampton University with a bachelor's degree in marketing in 1986 and worked as a contracting specialist at the National Security Agency before beginning stand-up in 1987 at a Washington, D.C., talent showcase. She came to national recognition as a writer and performer on The Chris Rock Show, sharing the 1999 Primetime Emmy Award for outstanding writing for a variety, music or comedy program, and Entertainment Weekly named her one of the twenty-five funniest people in America in 2004. Her recurring television work includes Curb Your Enthusiasm and The New Adventures of Old Christine, with Emmy-nominated guest roles on Black-ish and The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel, in which she played Moms Mabley. She has starred in her own specials and series, voices animated films, and since 2021 has starred in the Netflix sitcom The Upshaws. In 2024 she filmed a stand-up special at Hampton University's Ogden Hall, her alma mater.

name: W. C. Handy
aliases: William Christopher Handy; Father of the Blues
description: William Christopher Handy, born November 16, 1873, in Florence, Alabama, was the composer, cornetist, and bandleader who carried the blues from Black folk practice into published, orchestrated popular music. The son and grandson of Methodist ministers, he left home in 1892, worked with traveling musical groups, and from 1903 to 1921 conducted his own orchestra out of Clarksdale, Mississippi, steeping himself in the music of the Delta and Memphis. Unable to find a publisher, he co-founded the Pace and Handy Music Company, later Handy Brothers. His Memphis Blues, published in 1912, and above all St. Louis Blues in 1914, built blues harmony and the flattened blue seventh into songs the whole country could buy, play, and record; Beale Street Blues and Loveless Love followed. Handy also edited landmark anthologies of blues and spirituals and studies of Black musicians, and titled his 1941 autobiography Father of the Blues, the name by which he is still known. He died in New York on March 28, 1958.

name: Wesley Snipes
aliases: Wesley Trent Snipes; Eric Brooks / Blade (screen role)
description: Wesley Trent Snipes, born July 31, 1962, in Orlando, Florida, and raised in the Bronx, is an American actor, producer, martial artist, and author whose career spans more than forty years. Educated at the State University of New York at Purchase, where he earned a fine-arts degree, he broke through in the late 1980s and early 1990s with Major League, Spike Lee's Mo' Better Blues and Jungle Fever, and a star-making turn as Nino Brown in New Jack City. He consolidated that success in White Men Can't Jump and Passenger 57, won the Volpi Cup for Best Actor for One Night Stand in 1997, and formed Amen-Ra Films in 1991. His defining role came as Eric Brooks in Blade in 1998, reprised in two sequels and again in Deadpool & Wolverine in 2024. Trained from age twelve, he holds a fifth-dan black belt in Shotokan karate and a second-dan in Hapkido. He also debuted as a novelist with Talon of God in 2017, extending a career built on action stardom, dramatic range, and Black leading-man presence.

name: Wendell Smith
description: John Wendell Smith, born in Detroit, Michigan, in 1914, was an American sportswriter whose campaign to integrate Major League Baseball helped bring Jackie Robinson to the Brooklyn Dodgers in 1947. A graduate of West Virginia State College, he began at the Pittsburgh Courier in 1937 and was soon its sports editor, covering the Homestead Grays, Pittsburgh Crawfords, and Pittsburgh Pirates. After arranging a 1945 Boston Red Sox tryout for Robinson and two other Negro League players, he recommended Robinson to Dodgers president Branch Rickey, then travelled with Robinson in the minors in 1946 and with the Dodgers in 1947, rooming with him during spring training and writing the first Robinson biography. In August 1947 he joined the Chicago Herald-American, becoming one of the first Black sportswriters at a daily newspaper, and in 1948 he became the first Black member of the Baseball Writers' Association of America. He later wrote for the Chicago Sun-Times, broadcast for WGN, and campaigned in 1961 against segregated spring-training lodging. He died November 26, 1972, in Chicago, and in 1993 received the Hall of Fame's J.G. Taylor Spink Award posthumously.

name: Wendell Pierce
description: Wendell Pierce is an American actor and businessman from New Orleans, Louisiana, born December 8, 1963. Raised in Pontchartrain Park, a Black middle-class neighborhood built in the postwar era, he graduated from Benjamin Franklin High School and the New Orleans Center for Creative Arts in 1981 as a Presidential Scholar, then earned a Bachelor of Fine Arts from the Juilliard School's Drama Division in 1985. He first gained wide recognition as Detective William Bunk Moreland on HBO's The Wire (2002–2008), and played trombonist Antoine Batiste in Treme (2010–2013), also for HBO. His later television roles include attorney Robert Zane in Suits and James Greer in Tom Clancy's Jack Ryan, and from 2024 he has starred as Captain C. W. Wagner on Elsbeth. As a stage producer he won a Tony Award for Clybourne Park (2012), and he earned Olivier and Tony nominations playing Willy Loman in Death of a Salesman in London and on Broadway. After Hurricane Katrina flooded Pontchartrain Park in 2005, Pierce helped form the Pontchartrain Park Community Development Corporation to rebuild his childhood neighborhood with affordable, environmentally responsible homes.

name: Wes Moore
description: Wes Moore is an American politician, author and Army veteran serving as the 63rd governor of Maryland. Born October 15, 1978, in Takoma Park, Maryland, he moved with his family to the Bronx after his father's death when he was three, and returned to Maryland at age fourteen. He graduated from Valley Forge Military Academy and College with an associate's degree in 1998, earned a bachelor's degree at Johns Hopkins University, where he graduated Phi Beta Kappa and became the university's first Black Rhodes Scholar, and earned a master's degree in international relations at Oxford. In 2005 he deployed to Afghanistan with the 82nd Airborne Division, leading soldiers in combat, and afterward served as a White House Fellow. His 2010 book The Other Wes Moore became a perennial New York Times bestseller, and he later served four years as chief executive of the Robin Hood Foundation. Sworn in on January 18, 2023, Moore is Maryland's first Black governor in the state's 246-year history and the third African American elected governor in United States history.

name: Willie Mays
aliases: Willie Howard Mays Jr.; The Say Hey Kid; Say Hey Kid
description: Willie Howard Mays Jr., known as the Say Hey Kid, was an American center fielder born May 6, 1931, in Westfield, Alabama, and widely regarded as baseball's greatest all-around player. He played semiprofessional baseball at sixteen and joined the Birmingham Black Barons in 1948, playing only on Sundays during the school year. The New York Giants purchased his contract in 1950, and after minor-league seasons he reached the Giants in 1951 and was named Rookie of the Year. After Army service in 1952 to 1954, he returned to lead the league in hitting in 1954, help the Giants win the World Series, and make his celebrated over-the-shoulder catch in its opening game. He remained with the Giants through their move to San Francisco in 1958, was traded to the New York Mets in mid-1972, and retired after 1973. His career totals include a .301 batting average, 660 home runs, and 3,293 hits in Britannica's account, twelve consecutive Gold Gloves from 1957 to 1968, and two Most Valuable Player awards. Elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1979, he received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2015 and died June 18, 2024, in Palo Alto, California.

name: Wayne Miller
aliases: Wayne F. Miller; Wayne Forest Miller
description: Wayne F. Miller (1918–2013) was a Chicago-born American photographer whose documentary work after the Second World War produced one of the defining visual records of Black Chicago. The Art Institute of Chicago, which holds his work, lists him as born in 1918 and deceased in 2013, with South Side photographs dated 1946/48 among its holdings, including pool-hall and street scenes from that project. Miller called the series The Way of Life of the Northern Negro. The Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture holds a 1947 gelatin silver print from that series, depicting an unidentified couple in Chicago, and credits the image to Magnum Photos, with permission required for use. Published in book form as Chicago's South Side, 1946–1948 (2000), the photographs document the everyday life of a South Side community shaped by wartime migration from the South — its homes, churches, workplaces, and leisure — made by a photographer working inside the neighborhood over three postwar years. Miller's Chicago series is the basis of this record; his wider career in wartime and magazine photography is context, not the subject, and details beyond the opened institutional holdings are held for a fuller biographical pass.

name: Woman's Era
description: The Woman's Era was a Boston newspaper created by and for Black women, published under Josephine St. Pierre Ruffin, who served as its editor and publisher. It began as the newsletter of the Woman's Era Club, which Ruffin co-founded in Boston in 1893 with Maria Louise Baldwin, Ida B. Wells, and other Black women, a club devoted to education, anti-lynching work, and women's suffrage for Black Bostonians. In 1894 the paper began national distribution, and Massachusetts Women's History identifies it as the first national newspaper created by and for Black women. Through its pages Ruffin and her daughter Florida Ruffin Ridley publicized and organized the first National Conference of Colored Women in America, held in Boston in 1895, which drew one hundred women from twenty clubs across the country and produced the umbrella organization that later became the National Association of Colored Women's Clubs. Ruffin's tenure as editor and publisher is dated 1890 to 1897 in one account, a dating that conflicts with the 1894 national launch carried here and shown openly in this record's statistics. The paper is staged as a newspaper, the form its institutional histories consistently name, rather than as a magazine or journal.

name: Willie Lee Morrow
aliases: Willie Morrow; William Lee Morrow; Dr. Willie Morrow
description: Willie Lee Morrow (October 9, 1939 – June 22, 2022) was a San Diego barber, businessman, and inventor who built a Black hair-care enterprise from a Market Street barbershop. Born in Alabama to sharecropper parents, he moved to San Diego and opened his first salon there in 1959, after training as a barber and stylist. Inspired in 1962, National Public Radio reports, by a wide-toothed wooden comb brought from Nigeria, he taught himself to manufacture the comb that became known as the Afro pick, selling, at one point, twelve thousand a week. In 1969 the Pentagon hired him to teach military barbers how to cut and style Black hair. He founded the California Curl Company, whose California Curl treatment was the forerunner of the Jheri curl, wrote manuals on cutting and styling Black hair, and later founded the San Diego Monitor newspaper and a Black radio station. A 2016 museum exhibition in Escondido displayed more than two hundred and fifty objects from his collection of hair-care tools. Morrow died at his home in San Diego on June 22, 2022, aged eighty-two, and his daughter Cheryl succeeded him in the family businesses.

name: Wesley Morris
description: Wesley Morris is an American critic who serves as critic at large at The New York Times, where he writes about race and culture. A graduate of Yale University (class of 1997), he wrote for The San Francisco Chronicle and The San Francisco Examiner, then spent a stint as film critic at The Boston Globe, where he was awarded the Pulitzer Prize for Criticism in 2012. He subsequently worked as a staff writer and columnist for Grantland, writing about movies, television, and the role of style in professional sports, and joined The New York Times in 2015. In 2021 Morris won the Pulitzer Prize for Criticism a second time, for a series of essays exploring the intersection of race and pop culture — making him, per Colgate University's account of the Pulitzer record, the only writer to have won the Criticism prize more than once. The Pulitzer committee praised the 2021 work for its deeply engaged criticism on the intersection of race and culture in America, written in a singular style, alternately playful and profound. His subjects have ranged across the moral force of civilian cellphone videos, Hollywood's addiction to racial reconciliation fantasies, and the endangerment of romantic comedies. He has co-hosted the Times podcast Still Processing.

name: Willie Wells
aliases: Willie James Wells; El Diablo; The Devil
description: Willie Wells was a Negro leagues shortstop celebrated for range, sure hands, and power at a position then defined by defense. He starred for the St. Louis Stars, the Chicago American Giants, and the Newark Eagles, among other clubs, and played in Canada, Cuba, Mexico, and Puerto Rico, earning the nickname "El Diablo" in Mexico for his aggressive play. He was selected eight times for the East-West Classic, first played in 1933, and the Handbook of Texas calls him an extraordinary fielder, nicknamed in his playing days the Shakespeare of Shortstops. After a concussion he adopted a construction hard hat at the plate, an early batting-helmet precedent. He later served as a player-manager, notably with Newark, and mentored younger players, working with Jackie Robinson on his double-play turn. Wells played professionally from 1924 to 1948. He died January 22, 1989, in Austin, Texas, and was posthumously inducted into the National Baseball Hall of Fame in 1997.

name: WVON 40 Under 40 Game Changers
aliases: 40 Under 40 Game Changers; WVON Game Changers; COMPASS: The Navigators of Next
description: WVON's 40 Under 40 Game Changers is the Chicago Black talk station's honor program recognizing dynamic leaders under 40 who are making meaningful impact across Chicago and beyond — in business, innovation, community, culture, media, health, education and civic leadership. Eligibility, per the program: nominees must be 39 years old or younger by the eligibility deadline and demonstrate Chicago impact, leadership, innovation or service, and community influence. The program is sponsored by BMO. Its 2026 edition runs under the theme 'COMPASS: The Navigators of Next'; the Class of 2026 as published names 43 honorees — three more than the '40' brand, a discrepancy this record states rather than smooths — and the class is celebrated on Thursday, October 29, 2026, with a keynote by Dr. Louis Carr, President of BET. The program site publishes no celebration venue.
